reference: RFC 8785, JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS), IETF, June 2020
numeric_policy: Floats are refused, not formatted. RFC 8785 defers number serialisation to ECMAScript Number::toString, whose shortest-round-trip double formatting is the usual place two languages drift. Every quantity in this project that was a float is derived from integers that already exist upstream, so it is carried as Ratio{n,d} (exact) or Fixed6{v,scale} (quantised once, at the boundary). The consequence is that a conforming implementation needs no float formatter at all.

Ratio.rule: stored reduced, so 1024/524288 and 1/512 are the same bytes

Decimal6.json: a JSON string with exactly six decimal places
Decimal6.rule: copied verbatim from the engine's report; never reformatted, never re-rounded. Matches core/ledger/src/jcs.rs.

must_reject.why: a float anywhere in the payload
a float nested in an array
integer beyond 2^53-1 (a double cannot hold it)
Decimal6 that is not exactly six decimal places

not_exercised.lone_surrogate_in_key: Python cannot hold an unpaired surrogate in a str without surrogatepass, and no SentinelWipe key contains one. UNVERIFIED in both implementations; if a key ever arrives from an external source this becomes reachable and must be tested first.
not_exercised.numbers_outside_i64: No field in this project exceeds i64. The 2^53 ceiling binds first and is tested.

cases.name: empty_object
cases.note: the base case both implementations get wrong first

cases.name: key_order_ascii
cases.note: empty string sorts first; uppercase before lowercase

cases.name: key_order_utf16_astral
cases.note: U+1F600 is the surrogate pair D83D DE00 and must sort BEFORE U+FFFD. Code-point ordering puts it after. This vector is the entire reason RFC 8785 3.2.3 specifies UTF-16 code unit rather than code point.

cases.name: escapes_control_u
cases.note: below 0x20 with no short form -> \u00xx, lowercase hex

cases.name: escapes_nonascii_bare
cases.note: non-ASCII is emitted as itself, never \u

cases.name: ratio_rate_bps
cases.note: bytes per second as bytes over nanoseconds, both integers upstream

cases.name: ratio_structural_headroom
cases.note: (0.75-0.65)/0.35 is exactly 1/28. Carrying 0.035714 discarded the fact that it is exact and invited a rounding argument on stage.

cases.name: decimal6_entropy_before
cases.note: a measured continuous value, verbatim from the engine's report

cases.name: decimal6_is_a_json_string
cases.note: carried as a STRING, not a number. A scaled integer would need a rounding step, and Python rounds half-even while Rust rounds half-away-from-zero: they differ only on an exact .5 at the sixth decimal, which is exactly the kind of divergence that surfaces for the first time on a verifier's machine.

cases.name: certificate_skeleton
cases.note: the real shape. A conforming Rust implementation must produce these exact bytes.
